extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students addressing proof of damages in patent-infringement cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the kinds of evidence and legal rules for proving and measuring damages (and profits) in patent-infringement suits, including when license royalties, plaintiff loss, or defendant profits are appropriate measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: License fee as conclusive measure when license corresponds to the infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: When the evidence discloses that a license fee has been established and that the defendant's acts of infringement have been such as in quality and extent were contemplated by the license to which the fee has been attached, the amount of this fee as it existed at the date of the infringement, with interest from that date, must be taken by the jury as conclusive proof of the actual damages to which the plaintiff is entitled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The license fee is the sum the plaintiff has offered to accept and the jury should ratify it; it is immaterial whether the defendant profited or the plaintiff was prejudiced — such evidence is inadmissible to alter damages computed on the license fee basis. (Cases cited: Seymour v. McCormick, Wooster v. Thornton, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment required when a gross license covers multiple patents/claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a gross license fee covers more than one invention or many patents, and the defendant infringes only some claims or one claim, the license fee is not a proper measure of damages unless it can be fairly apportioned to the infringed claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the license cannot be shown to have been paid for the specific claim in question, the royalty may be irrelevant and nominal damages only may be recoverable. Examples: cases where rescinded contracts or whole-machine licenses were not usable without proof of proportionate value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using later-established license fees
rubrics_metrics.description: A license fee established after the infringement is not a conclusive measure of damages, though it may be considered and is a question of fact whether the value at the infringement date equaled the subsequent license fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may consider a post-infringement license fee but should treat its equality to past value as factual and not automatic. (See Wooster v. Thornton.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of license terms (discounts, prompt-payment) on measured damages
rubrics_metrics.description: A license fee fixed at a given rate with discounts (e.g., for prompt payment) is to be taken as fixing the lower rate as the true measure of damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License payment terms may define the proper royalty measure; courts have treated such terms as determinative for the lower bound of recoverable damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow interest on license fees when used as measure
rubrics_metrics.description: When license fees are taken as the measure of damages, interest from the date of the infringement must be allowed on those fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions support awarding interest on royalties used to measure actual damages. (See Creamer v. Bowers; Sickels v. Borden.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two forms of exclusive enjoyment and their measures of pecuniary value
rubrics_metrics.description: Monopoly enjoyed by exclusive practice of an invention takes two principal forms: (1) use of the invention in the plaintiff's business and sale of its products (common for processes, designs, machines) — measured by the advantage conferred (improved quality, lower cost, greater sales or higher profits); (2) making and sale of the patented articles (common for manufactures/compositions) — measured by the difference between expense of production and price obtained (unit profit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the invention is an improvement, the form of enjoyment follows the original; both forms permit evidence of market value (e.g., license fees, prices on sales) to estimate damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct evidence of injury — proof of reduction in plaintiff's sales or prices
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct evidence of the plaintiff's injury consists of testimony showing the plaintiff's sales or prices before the invasion of rights and the decrease in either which resulted from the infringement (e.g., customers diverted, defendant supplying plaintiff's former market, inferiority harming plaintiff's reputation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of admissible direct evidence: proof customers were diverted, plaintiff forced to lower prices, goods made but unsold due to competition. Remote, contingent, or speculative losses that cannot be distinctly traced to the infringement are not admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect evidence of injury — defendant's profits as a proxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect evidence of the plaintiff's injury may be afforded by the profits resulting to the defendant from the use of the invention during the infringement; such profits are a fact the jury may consider in estimating the plaintiff's loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no presumption that defendant's profits equal plaintiff's loss. Profits are admissible especially where plaintiff was ready and able to supply the market and would likely have sold what defendant sold; however, courts must deduct value attributable to other patented devices in defendant's product and consider other causes. If the defendant's enterprise was unprofitable or the infringement inseparable from broader business losses/gains, profits may be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages are measured by plaintiff's actual loss, not defendant's theoretical gains
rubrics_metrics.description: The true measure of damages is the loss the plaintiff sustained by reason of the infringement, not what the defendant made or might have made by the unlawful use of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Juries must gather plaintiff loss from evidence (e.g., diverted customers, prevented sales). Courts have repeatedly rejected equating defendant gains with plaintiff damages absent proof linking them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When plaintiff manufactures and defendant's sales displace plaintiff, entire loss imputable to defendant (with allowances)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff makes and sells articles that are unsalable without the patented invention, and the defendant sells infringing articles compelling the plaintiff to lower prices, the entire loss is imputable to the defendant, subject to proper allowance for other patented devices contained in the defendant's article and for other advantages the defendant enjoyed in selling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Yale Lock Co. v. Sargent and Fitch v. Bragg: the plaintiff may recover the full diminution in profit after apportioning value of non-infringing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of proving causal link for price reduction or lost sales
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss by reduction of prices or reduction of sales must be proved to be due solely or to a definite extent to the defendant's infringement; conjecture is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plaintiff had begun reducing prices before the infringement, or multiple causes could explain the decline, the claimed loss must be specifically attributed to the defendant's acts (see Comely v. Marckwald).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits recovery sometimes independent of established royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits may be recovered for the use of the invention without reference to the usual royalty, i.e., a plaintiff may seek the defendant's profits instead of a royalty measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity and law differ in methods; some cases allow accounting for defendant gains even when no license existed (e.g., Knox v. Great Western Quicksilver), but courts carefully scrutinize separability and apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of equitable profit-accounting methods must be reconciled with legal measure of damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods proper in equity (accounting for all gains and savings the infringer obtained) have sometimes been used to show defendant advantage, but damages at law are governed by different rules and require proof of plaintiff loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where equity-style measures (including savings from avoided losses) are employed, courts caution against automatically converting those into legal damages without connecting plaintiff's loss; juries should consider but not treat such measures as conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of market value: license fees, sale prices, and testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the invention to the plaintiff may be shown by evidence such as existing license fees, prices on sales, and testimony about utility and advantage over old devices; such evidence is appropriate where no established royalty exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of an established royalty, general evidence of utility and advantage is resorted to in order to approximate a fair measure of damages (see Suffolk Co. v. Hayden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote or contingent losses not admissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of remote or contingent losses which cannot be measured by the difference between what the plaintiff would have cleared but for the infringement and what he actually received is not admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts exclude speculative damages; recoverable losses must be demonstrable and fairly traceable to the infringement (see Carter v. Baker and related cases).
